# Design: OpenAI Privacy Filter as Optional Redaction Add-on

**Status:** Draft
**Date:** 2026-05-12
**Author:** Peyton Montei
**Worktree branch:** `openai-redact`

## Context

The `redact` package ([redact/redact.go](../../../redact/redact.go)) runs seven
deterministic detection layers that produce a single merged set of
`taggedRegion`s before substitution:

1. Entropy-based (`secretPattern` + Shannon entropy, threshold 4.5) — always on
2. Pattern-based (`betterleaks`, ~260 known formats) — always on
3. Credentialed URIs (`REDACTED`) — always on
4. Database connection strings (JDBC, keyword DSN, semicolon DSN) — always on
5. User-defined custom rules (inline + rule packs) — opt-in
6. Bounded credential key/value pairs (`DB_PASSWORD=REDACTED — always on
7. Regex-based PII (email, phone, address, custom regex) — opt-in via `ConfigurePII`

Every layer is regex/entropy and microseconds per call. The detector runs on
every checkpoint write — per-turn temporary checkpoints on the shadow branch,
condensation to `entire/checkpoints/v1` on commit, and read-side export paths
(`entire attach`, `entire explain`, `entire doctor bundle`). The
`RedactedBytes` type enforces at compile time that downstream consumers
(checkpoint stores, `compact.Compact`) only see redacted bytes.

The pipeline has a known weak area: contextual PII that regex cannot reason
about — most notably **personal names**. The existing regex PII layer covers
email/phone/address by shape, not by context, and has no detector for
person names at all. Teams that want stronger PII coverage today must either
accept the gap or write per-name custom rules, which scales poorly.

OpenAI released [openai/privacy-filter](https://github.com/openai/privacy-filter)
on 2026-04-17. It is a 1.5B-parameter (50M active, MoE) bidirectional
token-classification model, Apache 2.0, that labels text into 8 categories:

- `account_number`, `secret` — overlap heavily with betterleaks + entropy
- `private_email`, `private_phone`, `private_address` — overlap with our regex PII
- `private_url`, `private_date` — partial / no existing coverage
- `private_person` — **no existing coverage; the unique capability**

The model ships as a Python CLI (`opf`) and a Python API. Weights download
to `~/.opf/privacy_filter` on first run (~1.5 GB). There is no `serve` mode
today; invocations are one-shot. The model card explicitly lists
"over-redaction of benign high-entropy strings, placeholders, hashes, sample
credentials, or synthetic examples that resemble secrets" as a documented
failure mode — i.e., layering its `secret` category on top of our existing
secret detectors would re-introduce exactly the over-redaction problem the
project has already tuned away.

### Constraints carried from prior incidents

- **Over-redaction makes logs unusable.** Prior versions of the redaction
  pipeline were too aggressive; users could not read their own transcripts.
  Every layer added must avoid regressing this.
- **Push paths are already long.** Condensation and push add latency to
  every commit. Adding an unbounded ML call inline to every per-turn write
  is a non-starter.
- **Opt-in framing.** This feature is for teams that want stronger PII
  coverage and are willing to install an extra dependency. Default behavior
  for users who do nothing must not change.

## Goals

1. Add OpenAI Privacy Filter as an optional eighth detection layer that
   augments — never replaces — the existing seven.
2. Run OPF only at the boundaries where redacted bytes leave per-turn local
   state: condensation to `entire/checkpoints/v1`, and the read-side export
   paths (`attach`, `explain`, `doctor bundle`). Per-turn temporary writes
   stay on the fast pipeline.
3. Default category set is `private_person` only — the genuine new
   capability — with all seven other categories individually toggleable but
   off by default.
4. Fail soft. If OPF is unavailable, crashes, or times out, log an
   actionable warning and fall back to the full existing seven-layer stack.
   Never block the commit/push for an opt-in add-on. Teams that want strict
   guarantees can flip `on_failure: "block"`.
5. Keep the runtime adapter behind an interface so we can swap shell-out
   for daemon-mode later without churning the detector or any callsite.

## Non-goals

- **Replacing any existing layer.** Betterleaks, entropy, custom rules, and
  the regex PII layer all keep running unchanged.
- **Auto-installing OPF.** The user runs `pip install` themselves. We do
  not ship Python, manage a venv, or download weights.
- **Shipping daemon mode in this iteration.** Documented as a follow-up;
  the interface boundary is designed to accept it.
- **Adding new top-level config keys.** OPF settings live as a sibling
  inside the existing `RedactionSettings`.
- **Changing default behavior for users who do nothing.** Zero impact if
  `redaction.openai_privacy_filter` is absent from settings.

## Approach

OPF becomes **layer 8** in `redact.String` — a region producer that emits
`taggedRegion` entries and rides the existing merge-and-replace machinery
([redact.go:235-265](../../../redact/redact.go)) for free.

To keep per-turn writes off the model, the package exposes two entry-point
pairs:

```go
// Existing — fast, always-on. Called by every per-turn write path.
func String(s string) string
func JSONLBytes(b []byte) (RedactedBytes, error)

// New — fast layers + OPF augmentation. Called only by condensation + export.
func StringWithPrivacyFilter(ctx context.Context, s string) string
func JSONLBytesWithPrivacyFilter(ctx context.Context, b []byte) (RedactedBytes, error)
```

Splitting at the entry-point level (rather than via a context-scoped flag
on the existing functions) means every callsite that wants OPF says so by
name. `git grep WithPrivacyFilter` shows the entire augmented surface. The
plain entry points cannot accidentally activate OPF.

### Asymmetry vs. existing layers (intentional)

| Layer | Per-turn temp writes | Condensation | Export reads |
|---|---|---|---|
| Layers 1–7 (entropy, betterleaks, URIs, DB strings, custom rules, credential values, regex PII) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Layer 8 (OPF, when configured) | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |

This is safe for the **push threat model** because only
`entire/checkpoints/v1` is pushed, and condensation is the gateway to it.
Temporary shadow-branch checkpoints never leave the machine via push; they
do, however, get read out by export commands (`attach`, `explain`,
`doctor bundle`), so those callsites are also moved to the new entry
points.

## Settings schema

A new optional field on `RedactionSettings`
([settings/settings.go:159](../../../cmd/entire/cli/settings/settings.go)),
parallel to `PII` and `CustomRedactions`:

```jsonc
// .entire/settings.json
{
  "redaction": {
    "pii":               { /* existing, unchanged */ },
    "custom_redactions": { /* existing, unchanged */ },

    "openai_privacy_filter": {
      "enabled": false,                       // master switch; default off
      "categories": {                         // per-category opt-in; default all false
        "private_person":   true,             // the recommended default
        "private_email":    false,
        "private_phone":    false,
        "private_address":  false,
        "private_url":      false,
        "private_date":     false,
        "secret":           false,
        "account_number":   false
      },
      "command":         "opf",               // override if not on PATH or pinned to a venv
      "timeout_seconds": 30,                  // per-call hard timeout
      "on_failure":      "warn"               // "warn" | "block"; default "warn"
    }
  }
}
```

Go struct mirroring the schema:

```go
type RedactionSettings struct {
    PII                 *PIISettings      `json:"pii,omitempty"`
    CustomRedactions    map[string]string `json:"custom_redactions,omitempty"`
    OpenAIPrivacyFilter *OPFSettings      `json:"openai_privacy_filter,omitempty"`
}

type OPFSettings struct {
    Enabled        bool            `json:"enabled"`
    Categories     map[string]bool `json:"categories,omitempty"`
    Command        string          `json:"command,omitempty"`         // default "opf"
    TimeoutSeconds int             `json:"timeout_seconds,omitempty"` // default 30
    OnFailure      string          `json:"on_failure,omitempty"`      // default "warn"
}
```

### Design choices, justified

- **Settings.json (committed), not settings.local.json.** Redaction
  *policy* is a team decision; install state is per-machine. The `"warn"`
  default protects devs who have not run `pip install opf` — they see a
  warning, condensation proceeds with layers 1–7, push works. The existing
  settings merge already supports per-machine override via
  `.entire/settings.local.json`.
- **Category strings match OPF's output labels exactly** (`private_person`,
  not `person`). `grep private_person` shows config and OPF JSON output
  with one query.
- **Two-step opt-in.** Adding the block does nothing until both `enabled`
  is true and at least one category is true. Matches the "optional
  add-on" framing.
- **`command` lets users pin to a venv** (e.g.,
  `/Users/alice/.venvs/opf/bin/opf`) without polluting PATH.
- **No environment variable overrides.** Consistent with the existing
  `ConfigurePII` / `ConfigureCustomRules` precedent.
- **Categories as `map[string]bool`, not struct fields with `*bool`.** OPF's
  taxonomy could grow (fine-tuning to add labels is supported). A map
  handles new categories without a `settings.go` change.

### Discovery surface

`entire configure --opf` interactive flow (mirrors existing `entire
configure` pattern; not required for v1, removes friction for the default
case):

1. Check if `opf` is on PATH; print install instructions if not.
2. Walk through the eight categories with descriptions.
3. Write the result to `.entire/settings.json`.

## Output format: OPF labels → existing replacement tokens

OPF emits spans like `[{"start": 12, "end": 17, "label": "private_person"}]`.
Mapping these to the existing `taggedRegion.label` field — where empty
produces bare `REDACTED` and non-empty produces `[REDACTED_<LABEL>]` per
[redact.go:196-200](../../../redact/redact.go) — is one table:

| OPF label | `taggedRegion.label` | Rendered token |
|---|---|---|
| `private_person` | `PERSON` | `[REDACTED_PERSON]` |
| `private_email` | `EMAIL` | `[REDACTED_EMAIL]` (matches existing regex PII) |
| `private_phone` | `PHONE` | `[REDACTED_PHONE]` (matches existing regex PII) |
| `private_address` | `ADDRESS` | `[REDACTED_ADDRESS]` (matches existing regex PII) |
| `private_url` | `URL` | `[REDACTED_URL]` |
| `private_date` | `DATE` | `[REDACTED_DATE]` |
| `account_number` | `ACCOUNT_NUMBER` | `[REDACTED_ACCOUNT_NUMBER]` |
| `secret` | `""` (empty) | `REDACTED` (bare, matches betterleaks/entropy) |

Labeled tokens (rather than bare `REDACTED` for every OPF hit) keep
"is this over-redaction?" feedback loops short — a human reading the
output can tell *why* something was redacted.

**Implementation footnote:** OPF returns spans against its tokenizer's
view of the text. The protocol adapter must verify whether the JSON
output uses character offsets or model-token offsets and, if the latter,
map them back to byte offsets at the adapter boundary. The
[OUTPUT_SCHEMAS.md](https://github.com/openai/privacy-filter/blob/main/OUTPUT_SCHEMAS.md)
document in the OPF repo is the source of truth.

## Progress UX and failure messages

Condensation runs inside the PostCommit hook
([strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go](../../../cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go)).
Stdout/stderr from that hook is visible to the user's terminal.

### Progress messages

**TTY, non-accessible (default):**

```
→ OpenAI Privacy Filter: scanning transcript…
✓ OpenAI Privacy Filter: done (1.8s)
```

Both lines persist in scrollback — the "done" line is a receipt that
the security-sensitive opt-in feature actually ran. Silent success
should not look identical to silent skip.

**Non-TTY (redirected, piped, CI):**

```
[entire] redaction: openai privacy filter scanning transcript (this may take a few seconds)
[entire] redaction: openai privacy filter completed in 1.8s
```

**`ACCESSIBLE=1`:** Same as non-TTY — plain text, no spinner, no
carriage returns. Matches the accessibility pattern already documented
in `CLAUDE.md`.

### Failure messages (actionable, one line per cause)

| Failure | Message |
|---|---|
| `opf` not on PATH | `× OpenAI Privacy Filter: 'opf' not found on PATH. Install with 'pip install opf' (see https://github.com/openai/privacy-filter) or set 'redaction.openai_privacy_filter.command' in .entire/settings.json. Falling back to default redaction layers.` |
| Spawn failed (permission, etc.) | `× OpenAI Privacy Filter: failed to spawn '<command>': <err>. Falling back to default redaction layers.` |
| Exceeded timeout | `× OpenAI Privacy Filter: exceeded <N>s timeout. Falling back to default redaction layers. Consider raising 'redaction.openai_privacy_filter.timeout_seconds' or disabling the filter.` |
| Non-zero exit / garbled stdout | `× OpenAI Privacy Filter: <command> exited with status <N>. Falling back to default redaction layers. Last stderr: <truncated>` |
| `on_failure: "block"` set | Same diagnostic + `Condensation aborted because on_failure is set to 'block'. Edit .entire/settings.json to change.` |

Every message:

- Names the feature unambiguously (`OpenAI Privacy Filter`, not `OPF`) so
  it is googleable.
- States what failed and what the user can do.
- States what happened to their data (`Falling back to default redaction
  layers.`) so trust is preserved.
- Goes to stderr; corrupting piped JSON output is unacceptable.

All messages also log through `slog.Warn` via the existing
`componentAttr = slog.String("component", "redaction")`
([custom.go:41](../../../redact/custom.go)) so `entire doctor logs`
shows them and `entire doctor bundle` captures them.

## Data flow / callsite audit

Every existing `redact.JSONLBytes` / `redact.String` callsite is
classified as **per-turn** (stays on the plain entry point) or
**condensation/export** (moves to the new entry point):

| Callsite | Classification | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `strategy/manual_commit_condensation.go:379` | Condensation — copies session → `entire/checkpoints/v1` | Switch to `JSONLBytesWithPrivacyFilter` |
| `strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go:2749` | Condensation — PostCommit transcript redaction | Switch to `JSONLBytesWithPrivacyFilter` |
| `strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go:2759` | Condensation — prompts during PostCommit | Switch to `StringWithPrivacyFilter` |
| `checkpoint/committed.go:205, 264, 729, 1776` | Condensation — invoked transitively | Switch to `*WithPrivacyFilter` |
| `checkpoint/committed.go:422, 840, 841, 859, 875, 1405` | Condensation — committed metadata fields | Switch to `StringWithPrivacyFilter` |
| `checkpoint/v2_committed.go:612, 906, 1018` | Condensation (v2 path) | Switch to `*WithPrivacyFilter` |
| `checkpoint/temporary.go:319, 390` | Per-turn temp write | **Stays on plain `JSONLBytes`** |
| `cli/attach.go:268` | Export read — reading stored transcript back out | Switch to `JSONLBytesWithPrivacyFilter` |
| `cli/explain.go:1111` | Export read — compacted transcript | Switch to `JSONLBytesWithPrivacyFilter` |
| `cli/doctor_bundle.go:260, 266` | Export bundle | Switch to both `JSONLContent` and `Bytes` variants |
| `cli/migrate.go:744, 1377, 1497, 1534` | Migration — `AlreadyRedacted` wrappers | **No change** — already-redacted bytes are not re-scanned |

### Configuration bootstrap

`strategy/common.go` already wires the existing redact configurators
([common.go:373, 400](../../../cmd/entire/cli/strategy/common.go)):

```go
redact.ConfigurePII(cfg)
redact.ConfigureCustomRules(redact.CustomRulesConfig{ ... })
```

Add a third sibling:

```go
if s.Redaction != nil && s.Redaction.OpenAIPrivacyFilter != nil {
    redact.ConfigurePrivacyFilter(redact.OPFConfig{
        Enabled:        s.Redaction.OpenAIPrivacyFilter.Enabled,
        Categories:     s.Redaction.OpenAIPrivacyFilter.Categories,
        Command:        s.Redaction.OpenAIPrivacyFilter.Command,
        TimeoutSeconds: s.Redaction.OpenAIPrivacyFilter.TimeoutSeconds,
        OnFailure:      s.Redaction.OpenAIPrivacyFilter.OnFailure,
    })
}
```

Single config call at startup; later calls to `*WithPrivacyFilter` read it
through a guarded global the same way `getPIIConfig()` and
`getCustomRulesConfig()` do today.

## Package layout

One new file in the `redact/` package plus one stand-alone runtime
adapter under a sub-package:

```
redact/
├── redact.go                 (existing — regions, merge, JSONL machinery; +1 entry-point pair)
├── pii.go                    (existing — regex PII detector)
├── custom.go                 (existing — user rules)
├── packs.go                  (existing — rule packs)
├── opf.go                    (NEW — OPF detector layer + config + label mapping)
└── opf_runtime/
    ├── runtime.go            (NEW — interface: Redact(ctx, text, categories) → []Span)
    ├── shellout.go           (NEW v1 — exec.Command implementation)
    └── daemon.go             (FUTURE — only if benchmark shows daemon is worth it)
```

`redact/opf_runtime/runtime.go`:

```go
type Runtime interface {
    Redact(ctx context.Context, text string, categories []string) ([]Span, error)
    Close() error
}

type Span struct {
    Start int
    End   int
    Label string  // OPF's label, e.g. "private_person"
}
```

`shellout.go` spawns `opf` per call, talks JSON on stdin/stdout, respects
context cancellation. ~100–150 LOC. A future `daemon.go` would implement
the same interface; the constructor in `opf.go` picks one based on
settings. **No changes to `redact/opf.go` or any callsite when the
runtime is swapped.**

## Runtime decision (deferred to benchmark)

Shell-out (per-call cold-start of Python + weight load) vs daemon-mode
(load once, serve over a unix socket) is the largest remaining unknown.
The benchmark plan to resolve it:

1. Install OPF locally: clone `openai/privacy-filter`, `pip install -e .`,
   let weights download to `~/.opf/privacy_filter` (~1.5 GB, one-time).
2. Pick a representative input: reuse
   `cmd/entire/cli/transcript/compact/testdata/claude_full2.jsonl` so
   numbers compare directly to `BenchmarkRedactJSONLBytes`.
3. Three measurements:
   - **Cold shell-out:** `time opf -f claude_full2.jsonl`, three fresh shells, median.
   - **Warm in-process:** 30-line Python script that imports `opf._api`, loads model once, redacts the fixture 5 times in a loop. Time per call after the first.
   - **Pure Python startup:** `time python -c 'import opf'` as a sanity check.
4. Decision rule:
   - `cold − warm` > 2s **and** frequent condensations per session → daemon pays off.
   - `cold − warm` < 500ms → ship shell-out; daemon is busywork.
   - In between → judgment call; lean shell-out for time-to-ship.

A useful third data point: time the *entire current condensation*
end-to-end on a real session with no OPF, to know how big the latency
budget is. If condensation already takes 800ms, adding 2s of OPF
cold-start triples it; adding 200ms is noise.

The runtime choice is **decoupled from every other part of this design**.
Settings, integration point, replacement tokens, UX, failure handling —
none depend on shell-out vs daemon. The decision is made before writing
the runtime adapter, not before approving this spec.

## Testing strategy

Three concentric rings mapping onto how the existing `redact` package is
tested:

### Ring 1 — Unit tests in `redact/opf_test.go` (no `opf` binary required)

A fake `opf_runtime.Runtime` returns canned spans. Verifies:

- `ConfigurePrivacyFilter` correctly thresholds enabled/disabled.
- Disabled config → `detectOPF` returns nil with zero runtime calls.
- Span-to-`taggedRegion` mapping is correct for each of the 8 OPF labels.
- OPF regions merge correctly with regions from other layers (overlap
  with entropy hit, overlap with betterleaks hit, label-tie-break
  determinism).
- Failure modes: runtime returns error → no panic, regions returned are
  nil; `on_failure: "block"` propagates; `"warn"` does not.
- Categories filter: if `private_person: true` but runtime returns a
  `private_email` span anyway, that span is dropped.

### Ring 2 — Adapter contract tests in `redact/opf_runtime/` (no `opf` binary required)

A stub binary in `testdata/fake-opf.sh` that the shell-out runtime
invokes. Verifies:

- Request format we send matches what `opf` accepts.
- Response format we accept matches what `opf` documents.
- Timeout cancellation kills the child and returns context error.
- Non-zero exit / garbled JSON / empty stdout all become typed errors.
- The `command` setting overrides the binary path.
- Stderr from the child is captured into the error message.

### Ring 3 — Integration tests gated by `OPF_BIN` env var (skipped in CI)

`//go:build opf_integration` so they only run when explicitly invoked:

```go
func TestOPF_LiveBinary(t *testing.T) {
    if os.Getenv("OPF_BIN") == "" {
        t.Skip("set OPF_BIN to run live OPF integration tests")
    }
    // redact a real fixture; assert private_person spans match expected
}
```

A handful of these catch protocol drift if OPF upstream changes its
output format. Devs with OPF installed run them locally; CI does not
pay the install/download cost.

### Benchmark

Extend `redact_bench_test.go`:

- `BenchmarkRedactJSONLBytesWithPrivacyFilter` with a fake runtime —
  measures adapter overhead, not OPF inference; stable enough to compare
  across branches.
- A separate `//go:build opf_integration` benchmark measures real
  wall-clock cost.

## Risks and mitigations

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| OPF over-redacts in practice on real transcripts | `private_person` default keeps the surface narrow; users opt up; failure path always falls back to layers 1–7; documented in error messages so users can disable cleanly. |
| Cold-start latency makes commits feel sluggish | Latency budget known via the benchmark before implementation; daemon mode is a contained follow-up with no API churn. |
| OPF upstream changes JSON output schema | Ring 2 stub tests pin our protocol expectations; Ring 3 live tests detect drift; failure path falls back rather than crashing. |
| User has OPF enabled on machine A, syncs repo to machine B without `opf` installed | `on_failure: "warn"` default lets B proceed with layers 1–7; clear actionable error tells them what to install. |
| Two condensations race on the same machine and both spawn `opf` | Shell-out version is naturally isolated (separate processes); future daemon needs lock-per-socket — noted in the daemon design when we get there. |
| OPF labels span boundaries differently from regex layers | The existing `taggedRegion` merge machinery already resolves overlapping regions deterministically; labels follow first-region-wins, regions follow widest-wins. |

## Open questions

1. Does the OPF JSON output schema return character offsets or model-token
   offsets? Verify against
   [OUTPUT_SCHEMAS.md](https://github.com/openai/privacy-filter/blob/main/OUTPUT_SCHEMAS.md)
   before writing the adapter. If tokens, the adapter does the
   token-to-byte mapping; not visible to the rest of the package.
2. Should `entire configure --opf` ship in the same iteration, or as a
   follow-up? My recommendation is follow-up — the JSON schema is small
   enough to hand-edit, and shipping the detector with a working failure
   message is more valuable than shipping a configure helper.
3. Whether to also surface a one-line summary in `entire status` ("OpenAI
   Privacy Filter: enabled (private_person)") so users can confirm it is
   active without opening settings. Cheap to add; deferred unless asked.

## Out of scope for this iteration

- Daemon mode runtime (the `daemon.go` placeholder).
- Auto-install / venv management.
- Fine-tuning OPF on team-specific data — supported by upstream, not
  wired into this CLI.
- Surfacing per-category accuracy metrics in `entire doctor`.
- Cross-platform Windows packaging concerns for daemon mode (when we get
  there).

Good catch — looking at OPF's own sample data tells a different story than I framed in the spec.

## What OPF considers `secret` (their public examples)

Only three concrete examples exist in the public repo:

| Example | Context where it appeared |
|---|---|
| `sk-test-XYZ987` | "Reset credentials at … and **rotate secret** sk-test-XYZ987." |
| `Priv4cy-Filt3r-2026` | "Support ticket notes: … and **passphrase** Priv4cy-Filt3r-2026." |
| `QK-TST-000-BDX5YNAL` | "Record test_000 includes **marker** QK-TST-000-BDX5YNAL and must be archived." (fine-tuning demo) |

And one `account_number`:
- `40702810500001234567` — "you can **send a bill for account** 40702810500001234567."

## What this actually tells us

OPF's `secret` detector is **not** "any high-entropy string." It is **"a short opaque value that surrounding human prose called a secret/passphrase/token."** Look at the trigger words: "rotate secret", "passphrase", "marker". The model is picking up on the *context*, not the shape.

That means:

| Class of secret | Caught by today's stack | Caught by OPF? |
|---|---|---|
| OpenSSH private key blocks (`-----BEGIN…`) | ✅ betterleaks | Probably no — wrong shape |
| AWS keys (`AKIA…`) | ✅ betterleaks | Probably no |
| JWTs (`eyJ…`) | ✅ entropy + betterleaks | Probably no |
| 40-char SHA hashes | ✅ entropy | No — and our docs flag this as where OPF over-fires |
| `DB_PASSWORD=REDACTED env assignments | ✅ credential value layer | Maybe, if context is conversational |
| **"The new passphrase is XK-9217"** in chat | ❌ entropy might miss (low entropy) | ✅ **OPF's sweet spot** |
| **"please use access code 482-991"** | ❌ | ✅ Likely |
| **"my otp is 884213"** | ❌ | ✅ Likely |

The complementarity is more useful than I claimed in the spec. OPF's `secret` plugs the hole where humans *talk about* credentials in transcripts, which is exactly the agent-transcript content this repo deals with.

## Two other useful things I learned in the same look

1. **`OUTPUT_SCHEMAS.md` confirms spans are character offsets**, not model-token offsets (`"start": 0, "end": 5, "text": "Alice"`). That resolves **Open Question #1** in the spec — no token-to-byte mapping needed in the adapter.
2. **OPF's CLI emits its own placeholders** like `<PRIVATE_PERSON>` in its `redacted_text` field. We ignore that and consume the structured `detected_spans` instead, so our `[REDACTED_PERSON]` token stays consistent. Worth a one-line note in the spec.

## Suggested spec updates

Three small revisions, all in the same direction:

1. **Section 3 footnote / Open Question #1** — resolve: character offsets, no mapping needed.
2. **§Approach / risks table** — soften the framing that OPF's `secret` re-imports the over-redaction problem. It's still possible, but the model is more context-driven than I credited. Note that fixture-based testing during implementation is the gating step, not "skip this category by default."
3. **§Default categories** — leave `private_person` as the only default-true, **but** add a callout that `secret` is "likely safe to enable for agent-transcript workflows and worth turning on during the benchmark phase to measure false-positive rate against `claude_full2.jsonl`."

I'd recommend keeping the defaults conservative (still just `private_person`) and using the benchmark step to gather data on `secret` precision before recommending it as a default — but updating the spec to reflect that `secret` is a likely-good toggle, not a likely-problematic one.

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** This should be run in a dedicated worktree (created by brainstorming skill).

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (if subagents available) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## Remember
- Exact file paths always
- Complete code in plan (not "add validation")
- Exact commands with expected output
- Reference relevant skills with @ syntax
- DRY, YAGNI, TDD, frequent commits

## Plan Review Loop

After completing each chunk of the plan:

1. Dispatch plan-document-reviewer subagent (see plan-document-reviewer-prompt.md) with precisely crafted review context — never your session history. This keeps the reviewer focused on the plan, not your thought process.

3. If ✅ Approved: proceed to next chunk (or execution handoff if last chunk)

**Chunk boundaries:** Use `## Chunk N: <name>` headings to delimit chunks. Each chunk should be ≤1000 lines and logically self-contained.

**Review loop guidance:**
- Same agent that wrote the plan fixes it (preserves context)
- If loop exceeds 5 iterations, surface to human for guidance
- Reviewers are advisory - explain disagreements if you believe feedback is incorrect

## Execution Handoff

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Ready to execute?"**

Execute plan by dispatching fresh subagent per task, with two-stage review after each: spec compliance review first, then code quality review.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. ## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture, design, and review tasks**: use the most capable available model.

**Task complexity signals:**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## Handling Implementer Status

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Proceed to spec compliance review.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

## Advantages

**vs. Manual execution:**
- Subagents follow TDD naturally
- Fresh context per task (no confusion)
- Parallel-safe (subagents don't interfere)
- Subagent can ask questions (before AND during work)

**vs. Executing Plans:**
- Same session (no handoff)
- Continuous progress (no waiting)
- Review checkpoints automatic

**Efficiency gains:**
- No file reading overhead (controller provides full text)
- Controller curates exactly what context is needed
- Subagent gets complete information upfront
- Questions surfaced before work begins (not after)

**Quality gates:**
- Self-review catches issues before handoff
- Two-stage review: spec compliance, then code quality
- Review loops ensure fixes actually work
- Spec compliance prevents over/under-building
- Code quality ensures implementation is well-built

**Cost:**
- More subagent invocations (implementer + 2 reviewers per task)
- Controller does more prep work (extracting all tasks upfront)
- Review loops add iterations
- But catches issues early (cheaper than debugging later)

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Start implementation on main/master branch without explicit user consent
- Skip reviews (spec compliance OR code quality)
- Proceed with unfixed issues
- Dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts)
- Make subagent read plan file (provide full text instead)
- Skip scene-setting context (subagent needs to understand where task fits)
- Ignore subagent questions (answer before letting them proceed)
- Accept "close enough" on spec compliance (spec reviewer found issues = not done)
- Skip review loops (reviewer found issues = implementer fixes = review again)
- Let implementer self-review replace actual review (both are needed)
- **Start code quality review before spec compliance is ✅** (wrong order)
- Move to next task while either review has open issues

**If subagent asks questions:**
- Answer clearly and completely
- Provide additional context if needed
- Don't rush them into implementation

**If reviewer finds issues:**
- Implementer (same subagent) fixes them
- Reviewer reviews again
- Repeat until approved
- Don't skip the re-review

**If subagent fails task:**
- Dispatch fix subagent with specific instructions
- Don't try to fix manually (context pollution)
